report:
## Conclusion: No — regular vitamin C does **not** prevent colds for most people

Despite popular belief, the best available evidence says your answer should be **no**, not yes. Here's what the research shows:

**The key evidence:**

The **Cochrane review** (the gold standard for medical evidence) pooled 29 trials with 11,306 participants and found that in the general community (10,708 people), regular vitamin C supplementation had a risk ratio of **0.97 (95% CI 0.94–1.00)** for catching a cold — essentially **no meaningful prevention effect**. The review concluded that "long-term daily supplementation with vitamin C in large doses does not appear to prevent colds" ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold); [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23440782/)).

Germany's InformedHealth.org similarly states: "Taking vitamin C every day to try to prevent colds won't protect most people from colds" ([NCBI Bookshelf](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279544/)).

**What vitamin C *does* do:**

- It **slightly shortens cold duration**: ~8% in adults, ~14% in children ([MedlinePlus](https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/002145.htm); [Linus Pauling Institute](https://lpi.oregonstate.edu/mic/health-disease/common-cold)).
- A 2023 meta-analysis found a **15% reduction in cold severity** with ≥1 g/day ([BMC Public Health](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-023-17229-8)).
- It **may halve cold risk** in people under extreme physical stress (marathon runners, skiers, soldiers in subarctic conditions) ([Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000980_vitamin-c-preventing-and-treating-common-cold)).

**Bottom line:** For the general population, regular vitamin C intake does not prevent colds. It modestly reduces duration and severity once you're sick, and may help people under extreme physical stress.
